players.product: US T&D contractor - Hyosung HICO Breaker JV partner (US gas circuit breakers)

quarterly_data.signal: RECORD BACKLOG OF $53 BILLION - and the big work is not in it yet. Duke Austin: 'The record backlog we reported reflects the demand in front of us, but we're still in the early stages. The larger programs across the utility generation and technology load center markets are ahead of us, and we expect them to stack in the years to come.' The 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV transmission are still in engineering ('We're not in backlog on any of the bigger work yet'), and about 95% of the generation work is not in backlog either. He expects record backlog again in the third quarter and probably the fourth. Book-to-burn will be lumpy: 1:1 to 1:2 in ordinary quarters, 1:5 to 1:6 in quarters when big chunks of projects land (the 765 kV work brought in last quarter was that kind of boost) - 'lower lows and higher highs all the way through'. A large share of the technology work never touches backlog at all: MEP crews can 'book and bill $300 million on a site in a quarter' against an MSA and 'you never see it show up in backlog'. CFO Jayshree Desai on data-center backlog discipline: only items with limited notices to proceed go in, 'we don't put the rest in until the project is a confirmed go.'
quarterly_data.figure: Record total backlog $53B; ~95% of generation work not yet in backlog; up to $300M booked-and-burned on a single technology site per quarter, outside backlog

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 2026 meaningfully exceeded expectations: revenues $9.6 billion, adjusted EBITDA $1.1 billion - of which only about $11 million came from the four acquisitions closed during the quarter, so the beat was organic - net income attributable to common stock $451 million or $2.96 per diluted share, and adjusted diluted EPS $4.24, with double-digit growth in revenue, adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EPS. Quanta self-performs 80% to 85% of its work with more than 85,000 employees, which Duke Austin credits for record adjusted EPS in each of the last nine consecutive years. Balance sheet strengthened even while deploying capital on acquisitions: debt-to-EBITDA 1.7 (from 1.95 at the end of 2025), total liquidity approximately $2.8 billion, and a Moody's ratings upgrade.
quarterly_data.figure: Revenue $9.6B; adj EBITDA $1.1B (only $11M from acquisitions); adj diluted EPS $4.24; net income $451M / $2.96 GAAP; self-perform 80%-85%; debt/EBITDA 1.7

quarterly_data.signal: Full-year 2026 expectations raised across all metrics on the strong first half, better second-half visibility and the acquisitions: revenues $39.3 billion to $39.7 billion, adjusted EBITDA $4.1 billion to $4.2 billion, adjusted EPS $16.45 to $16.95, free cash flow $2 billion to $2.5 billion. Four companies were acquired after the Q1 release - Phalcon (Northeast fabrication), Enerfab, Percheron (right-of-way acquisition and permitting services; customer base is utilities and hyperscalers, essentially no Quanta revenue today, and it moves Quanta to the front end of both the technology pipeline and utility T&D) and PSD - for approximately $1.24 billion of upfront consideration net of cash plus approximately $242 million of contingent consideration. They contribute $1.2 billion to $1.4 billion of revenue and $120 million to $140 million of adjusted EBITDA to the raised guide, which the CFO said represents about six to seven months' worth and can be annualised from there. Duke Austin on the drivers: 'everything is moving upward at least close to double digits and some of it much greater' - electric is the biggest contributor, the renewables business is setting records, and the guide is deliberately prudent on weather and project slips.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue $39.3-39.7B; adj EBITDA $4.1-4.2B; adj EPS $16.45-16.95; FCF $2-2.5B; M&A adds $1.2-1.4B revenue / $120-140M EBITDA for $1.24B upfront + $242M contingent

quarterly_data.signal: Craft labour is NOT the binding constraint today - Duke Austin: 'We're nowhere near capacity.' More than 85,000 employees; roughly 15,500 people added over the past year, well over 7,000 of them organic with a significant portion in Q2; Quanta spends about $250 million a year on training. It takes about four years to make a craftsman and a journeyman, and he sees no oversupply of craft-skilled labour in the near future. Labour is fungible across segments - electricians and underground crews move between data-center work, industrial and gas compression work and T&D - which is where the acquisition synergies show up. Customers are securing craft as far out as their five- to seven-year capital plans, with 'decade-plus type arrangements out there'. Margin follows that utilisation: the electric segment can operate at 10% to 12% on the utility side, with 12% the utmost 'when you stack in large transmission and all aspects at once', and Duke sees room for further margin improvement in the second half.
quarterly_data.figure: 85,000+ employees, +15,500 over the year (>7,000 organic); ~$250M/yr training; 'nowhere near capacity'; electric segment margin range 10%-12% on the utility side

quarterly_data.signal: The stacking has not started. Duke Austin: the 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV projects and the generation work are 'just starting - a lot of it's in engineering'; they start hitting backlog in the later half of this year, crews go to the field around the second half of 2027, and the compounding effect then stacks out 'throughout what I would consider the decade' and 'well past 2030'. He compares it to 2012-2015, when a batch of big projects compounded, and says the base business is doing upper-single-digit to double-digit growth before any of that lands. The nearest concrete catalyst named on the call is the NiSource generation award: 'I do believe a significant amount of that will go into backlog in the third quarter.'
quarterly_data.figure: 765 kV / 345 kV / 500 kV plus generation work moves into backlog in the later half of 2026, into the field in the second half of 2027, stacking well past 2030; NiSource generation award expected to enter backlog in the third quarter

quarterly_data.signal: VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.
quarterly_data.figure: HICO high-voltage breaker JV plus owned transformer and utility-pole manufacturing; fabrication footprint ~seven million sq ft, +0.5 million sq ft from the recent acquisitions

quarterly_data.signal: Technology is now 15% to 20% of Quanta's business - 'a spectrum from chips to everything, not just data centers' - grown to that share over the last two years off the Cupertino Electric platform, and Duke Austin frames it as a second TAM 'every bit as big as our utility TAM'. Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.
quarterly_data.figure: Technology = 15% to 20% of the business; Quanta can self-perform 80% to 90% of a data-center build

quarterly_data.signal: WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)

It will cost less... much like we've done with AEP on 765.' Separately, the 765 kV work brought in last quarter gave backlog 'a big boost up', and he expects the 765 kV corridors plus 345 kV and 500 kV projects - today still in engineering - to move into backlog in the later half of 2026 and into the field in the second half of 2027, stacking through the decade.
